requirements: Show the contrast between physical confinement and the self/soul experienced as larger than confinement.
Provide the prisoner’s own realization rather than only a description of laughter.

evidence.sentence: They hold me captive.
My immortal soul?
Pierre glanced up at the sky and the twinkling stars in its faraway depths.
“And all that is me, all that is within me, and it is all I!” thought Pierre.
“And they caught all that and put it into a shed boarded up with planks!”

requirements: Show that witnessing unwilling people commit the killings destroys the witness’s sense of order or meaning.
Distinguish this collapse from guilt for his own wrongdoing or fear of his own execution alone.

evidence.sentence: Pierre did not understand that he was saved, that he and the rest had been brought there only to witness the execution.

From the moment Pierre had witnessed those terrible murders committed by men who did not wish to commit them, it was as if the mainspring of his life, on which everything depended and which made everything appear alive, had suddenly been wrenched out and everything had collapsed into a heap of meaningless rubbish.
Though he did not acknowledge it to himself, his faith in the right ordering of the universe, in humanity, in his own soul, and in God, had been destroyed.

When similar doubts had assailed him before, they had been the result of his own wrongdoing, and at the bottom of his heart he had felt that relief from his despair and from those doubts was to be found within himself.
But now he felt that the universe had crumbled before his eyes and only meaningless ruins remained, and this not by any fault of his own.

requirements: Show the release of Nicholas from his promise.
Explain Sonya’s hope that another marriage would bar his alternative match, preserving her own prospects.

evidence.sentence: She wrote that the last unfortunate events— the loss of almost the whole of the Rostovs’ Moscow property—and the countess’ repeatedly expressed wish that Nicholas should marry Princess Bolkonskaya, together with his silence and coldness of late, had all combined to make her decide to release him from his promise and set him completely free.

But when she heard of Prince Andrew’s presence in their house, despite her sincere pity for him and for Natasha, she was seized by a joyful and superstitious feeling that God did not intend her to be separated from Nicholas.
She knew that Natasha loved no one but Prince Andrew and had never ceased to love him.

She knew that being thrown together again under such terrible circumstances they would again fall in love with one another, and that Nicholas would then not be able to marry Princess Mary as they would be within the prohibited degrees of affinity.

requirements: Show the completed national/liberation mission.
Explain why the new European campaign requires a different leader and leaves the old commander no role.

evidence.sentence: Kutuzov alone would not see this and openly expressed his opinion that no fresh war could improve the position or add to the glory of Russia, but could only spoil and lower the glorious position that Russia had gained.
This being the field marshal’s frame of mind he was naturally regarded as merely a hindrance and obstacle to the impending war.

The movement of peoples from west to east was to be succeeded by a movement of peoples from east to west, and for this fresh war another leader was necessary, having qualities and views differing from Kutuzov’s and animated by different motives.
Alexander I was as necessary for the movement of the peoples from east to west and for the refixing of national frontiers as Kutuzov had been for the salvation and glory of Russia.
For the representative of the Russian people, after the enemy had been destroyed and Russia had been liberated and raised to the summit of her glory, there was nothing left to do as a Russian.

requirements: Show the host’s company as forced, artificial, or disappointing.
Contrast it with the sensible, quiet conversation beginning upon his departure.

evidence.sentence: Prince Andrew looked at the laughing Speranski with astonishment, regret, and disillusionment.
Everything that had formerly appeared mysterious and fascinating in Speranski suddenly became plain and unattractive.
But their gaiety seemed to Prince Andrew mirthless and tiresome.
Two letters brought by a courier were handed to Speranski and he took them to his study.
As soon as he had left the room the general merriment stopped and the guests began to converse sensibly and quietly with one another.

requirements: Show that the supposed earlier vision was invented.
Show later observation changing the remembered details and shared recollection reinforcing the apparent fulfillment.

evidence.sentence: She had in fact seen nothing then but had mentioned the first thing that came into her head, but what she had invented then seemed to her now as real as any other recollection.

She not only remembered what she had then said—that he turned to look at her and smiled and was covered with something red—but was firmly convinced that she had then seen and said that he was covered with a pink quilt and that his eyes were closed.
“Yes, yes, it really was pink!” cried Natasha, who now thought she too remembered the word pink being used, and saw in this the most extraordinary and mysterious part of the prediction.

requirements: Show recognition of the suffering enemy and their painful personal connection.
Show pity and a wider love overcoming the grievance, rather than merely recognizing the man.

evidence.sentence: In the miserable, sobbing, enfeebled man whose leg had just been amputated, he recognized Anatole Kuragin.
Yes, that man is somehow closely and painfully connected with me,” thought Prince Andrew, not yet clearly grasping what he saw before him.
He remembered everything, and ecstatic pity and love for that man overflowed his happy heart.
Prince Andrew could no longer restrain himself and wept tender loving tears for his fellow men, for himself, and for his own and their errors.

“Compassion,love of our brothers,for those who love us and for those who hate us, love of our enemies; yes, that love which God preached on earth and which Princess Mary taught me and I did not understand—that is what made me sorry to part with life, that is what remained for me had I lived.

requirements: Show the mother’s devastation by her son’s death.
Show the daughter regaining attachment to life through love and care for that mother.

evidence.sentence: For three weeks Natasha remained constantly at her mother’s side, sleeping on a lounge chair in her room, making her eat and drink, and talking to her incessantly because the mere sound of her tender, caressing tones soothed her mother.
Petya’s death had torn from her half her life.
When the news of Petya’s death had come she had been a fresh and vigorous woman of fifty, but a month later she left her room a listless old woman taking no interest in life.
But the same blow that almost killed the countess, this second blow, restored Natasha to life.
She thought her life was ended, but her love for her mother unexpectedly showed her that the essence of life—love—was still active within her.

requirements: Show musical absorption making money, honor, and other troubles seem unreal or irrelevant.
Show ordinary reality returning as soon as the song finishes.

evidence.sentence: And suddenly the whole world centered for him on anticipation of the next note, the next phrase, and everything in the world was divided into three beats: “Oh mio crudele affetto.”... One, two, three... one, two, three... One... “Oh mio crudele affetto.”... One, two, three... One.
“All this misery, and money, and Dolokhov, and anger, and honor—it’s all nonsense... but this is real... Now then, Natasha, now then, dearest!
But no sooner had Natasha finished her barcarolle than reality again presented itself.

requirements: Show avoidance of the companion’s appeal or gaze.
Show deliberate distraction or refusal to look back when the killing is indicated.

evidence.sentence: Karataev looked at Pierre with his kindly round eyes now filled with tears, evidently wishing him to come near that he might say something to him.
He made as if he did not notice that look and moved hastily away.
Karataev was still sitting at the side of the road under the birch tree and two Frenchmen were talking over his head.
From behind, where Karataev had been sitting, came the sound of a shot.
Pierre heard it plainly, but at that moment he remembered that he had not yet finished reckoning up how many stages still remained to Smolensk—a calculation he had begun before the marshal went by.

requirements: Show the suitor’s hesitation or failure to propose.
Show the father treating a nonexistent agreement as accomplished and the suitor accepting its inevitability.

evidence.sentence: “The step must be taken but I cannot, I cannot!” thought Pierre, and he again began speaking about indifferent matters, about Sergey Kuzmich, asking what the point of the story was as he had not heard it properly.
Pierre and Helene still sat talking just as before.

“My wife has told me everything!” (He put one arm around Pierre and the other around his daughter)—“My dear boy... Lelya... I am very pleased.” (His voice trembled) “I loved your father... and she will make you a good wife... God bless you!...” He embraced his daughter, and then again Pierre, and kissed him with his malodorous mouth.
“All this had to be and could not be otherwise,” thought Pierre, “so it is useless to ask whether it is good or bad.
Pierre held the hand of his betrothed in silence, looking at her beautiful bosom as it rose and fell.

requirements: Contrast his remembered death sentence with the actual hard-labor sentence.
Explain how this justifies giving the mob a victim and comforts his conscience through supposed public benefit.

evidence.sentence: Lightly swaying on the flexible springs of his carriage and no longer hearing the terrible sounds of the crowd, Rostopchin grew physically calm and, as always happens, as soon as he became physically tranquil his mind devised reasons why he should be mentally tranquil too.
This idea is le bien public, the hypothetical welfare of other people.

Not only did his reason not reproach him for what he had done, but he even found cause for self-satisfaction in having so successfully contrived to avail himself of a convenient opportunity to punish a criminal and at the same time pacify the mob.
“Vereshchagin was tried and condemned to death,” thought Rostopchin (though the Senate had only condemned Vereshchagin to hard labor), “he was a traitor and a spy.
I could not let him go unpunished and so I have killed two birds with one stone: to appease the mob I gave them a victim and at the same time punished a miscreant.”
